title: How browser pages work
runtime: Modern evergreen browser. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript fragments can be tried in a small local page or the browser DevTools described in the lesson.

objectives.text: Explain what the internet is and how data travels between devices.
Explain the browser, server, DNS, URL, HTTP request, and HTTP response in simple words.
Describe how HTML, CSS, and JavaScript become pixels and an interactive page.
Compare static generation, server-side rendering, client-side rendering, and hydration.
Use HTTP status codes and browser evidence to locate a failed resource or rendering problem.

learningFlow: Apply it to a fresh page

diagnostic.question: What is the difference between a browser and a web server?
diagnostic.answer: A browser requests and displays resources. A server receives requests and sends responses.

sections.title: What is the internet?
sections.body: The internet is a worldwide network of connected networks. Phones, laptops, routers, data centres, and many other devices exchange data by following shared networking rules called protocols. The web is one service that runs on the internet. Email, online games, voice calls, and the web can all use the internet without being the same thing. When you open a webpage, no single “internet computer” sends it; many networks cooperate to move data between your device and another device.

sections.title: How data travels
sections.body: Large data is divided into smaller units commonly called packets. Each packet carries addressing and ordering information so networking equipment can forward it toward the destination and the receiver can rebuild the data. IP handles addressing and routing between networks. Transport protocols handle delivery behavior: TCP provides an ordered reliable byte stream, while other transports make different tradeoffs. Your Wi-Fi or mobile connection reaches a router, then an internet provider, and often several intermediate networks before reaching the server. Packets for one response do not need to follow one physical cable or one identical route.

sections.title: What is a client?
sections.body: A client is software that requests or consumes a service. A browser is an HTTP client, but a mobile app, command-line tool, or another server can also be a client. The client chooses a URL, creates a request, sends headers and sometimes a body, waits for a response, then decides what to do with the result. “Client side” means work that runs on the user’s device, usually inside the browser for a web application.

sections.title: What is a server and how does it work?
sections.body: A server is software that listens for requests and sends responses; the word also commonly describes the computer running that software. A request first reaches an address and port. A web server or reverse proxy may handle TLS, caching, compression, and routing. Application code can then read the method, path, headers, identity, and body; validate input; read a database or another service; apply business rules; and create a response. The response contains a status code, headers, and usually a body. Servers can return stored files, generate HTML, or return data such as JSON.

sections.title: From a domain name to a server
sections.body: People use names such as example.com, while network connections need an address. DNS is a distributed naming system that resolves a host name to an IP address or another useful record. The browser, operating system, router, or resolver may reuse a cached answer. DNS does not download the page. It helps the client discover where to connect. HTTPS then protects the HTTP exchange in transit and lets the client verify the server identity through certificates.

sections.title: How a URL identifies a resource
sections.body: In https://shop.example:443/products/42?currency=INR#reviews, https is the scheme, shop.example is the host, 443 is an explicit port, /products/42 is the path, currency=INR is the query, and reviews is the fragment. The scheme affects how the client communicates. Host and port identify where to connect. Path and query help the server choose a resource or operation. The fragment is normally handled by the browser and is not sent in the HTTP request.

sections.title: What an HTTP request contains
sections.body: An HTTP request expresses an action. GET normally reads a representation, POST commonly submits or creates, PUT commonly replaces, PATCH changes part, and DELETE requests removal. The request includes a method, target path, headers, and sometimes a body. Headers describe facts such as accepted formats, authentication, caching, and content type. The method alone does not guarantee safe server behavior; the server implementation must follow the intended semantics and validate every untrusted value.

sections.title: What an HTTP response contains
sections.body: A response contains a status code, response headers, and optionally a body. Headers can describe the body type, caching, cookies, location, compression, and security policy. The body may be HTML, JSON, CSS, JavaScript, an image, or an error document. A successful transport does not prove that the returned data is correct, and a 200 response does not prove that later JavaScript will run without errors.

sections.title: HTTP status code groups
sections.body: Status codes have five groups. 100–199 are informational intermediate responses. 200–299 mean the request was handled successfully. 300–399 tell the client about redirection or another location. 400–499 mean the request cannot be fulfilled as sent or allowed; the server may still be healthy. 500–599 mean the server or an upstream service failed while handling a request. Always read the actual response because applications sometimes misuse codes.

sections.title: Common HTTP codes and what they mean
sections.body: 200 OK means the request succeeded. 201 Created means a new resource was created. 204 No Content means success with no response body. 301 and 308 are permanent redirects; 302 and 307 are temporary redirects, with method-preservation details differing by code. 304 Not Modified tells a cache that its stored representation can be reused. 400 Bad Request means invalid request syntax or input. 401 means authentication is required or invalid; despite its name, it is about authentication. 403 Forbidden means the server understood the identity or request but refuses access. 404 Not Found means the target resource was not found or is intentionally hidden. 405 Method Not Allowed means the path exists but rejects that method. 409 Conflict means the request conflicts with current state. 422 Unprocessable Content commonly means well-formed input failed semantic validation. 429 Too Many Requests means a rate limit was reached. 500 is a generic internal failure. 502 Bad Gateway means a gateway received a bad upstream response. 503 Service Unavailable usually means temporary overload or maintenance. 504 Gateway Timeout means an upstream response took too long.

sections.title: How files become a visible page
sections.body: The browser parses HTML into the DOM, a tree representing document nodes. It parses CSS and works out which declarations apply. DOM and style information contribute to a render tree. The browser calculates layout: each visible box’s size and position. It then paints pixels and composites layers. JavaScript can read or change the DOM and styles, which may trigger more style calculation, layout, paint, or compositing work. Linked CSS, scripts, fonts, images, and module imports create more requests. Parsing, downloading, and rendering can overlap; this is a pipeline, not one single step.

sections.title: Client-side rendering
sections.body: In client-side rendering, the first response can contain a small HTML shell and JavaScript. The browser downloads and runs the script, the application fetches data when needed, and JavaScript creates most page content in the DOM. CSR can support rich transitions after startup, but an empty shell, a large bundle, slow data requests, or a script failure can delay or prevent meaningful content. CSR describes where initial page HTML is produced; it does not mean the server is absent, because APIs and static files still come from servers.

sections.title: Server-side rendering and hydration
sections.body: With server-side rendering, application code creates useful HTML on the server for a request and sends that HTML to the browser. The user can often see meaningful content before the full client JavaScript runs. A React application may then hydrate: React attaches behavior to HTML that already represents the initial component output. Server and client output must match for reliable hydration. SSR can improve the first content experience and crawler access, but it adds server work, caching decisions, and the risk of slow server responses or hydration problems.

sections.title: Static generation and mixed rendering
sections.body: Static generation creates HTML before a user request, usually during a build. A CDN or simple server can then return the stored file quickly. It works well when many users can share the same content, but rebuilding or revalidation is needed when the source changes. Real applications often mix strategies: static marketing pages, server-rendered user pages, client-side interactions, and client fetches can exist together. Choose per route and data need instead of declaring one rendering method universally best.

sections.title: Debug the journey in order
sections.body: Start with observable evidence. In Network, find the document and linked resources, then inspect URL, method, status, content type, timing, request data, and response body. In Elements, check whether the expected DOM exists. In Console, begin with the first relevant error because later errors may be consequences. A 404 script points to a path or deployment problem; a 500 API response points to server handling; a 200 document followed by an exception points to client execution. Rendering strategy changes what “good initial HTML” should look like, so compare the response body with the live DOM.

examples.title: Read a URL
examples.explanation: The browser requests /products with a sort query, then moves to the reviews fragment after the page loads.
examples.tryThis: Change the path, query, and fragment. Explain which parts can affect the server request.

examples.title: See linked resources
examples.explanation: After the HTML arrives, the browser discovers and requests the CSS, JavaScript, and image.
examples.tryThis: Predict which missing file would remove styling, behavior, or the image.

examples.title: Read a request and response
examples.explanation: The request asks to read course data. The response reports success and identifies a JSON body. Real HTTP messages contain more details, but the same method, target, headers, status, and body model applies.
examples.tryThis: Change the response to 404 and write a useful error body. Explain which side chooses each value.

examples.title: Compare initial HTML
examples.code:
React course

Start with web foundations.
examples.explanation: The second response already contains meaningful markup. With an interactive React SSR app, client code hydrates matching HTML. Static HTML may need no hydration if it has no client behavior.
examples.tryThis: Disable JavaScript and predict what remains useful in each example.

practice.prompt: Split this URL into scheme, host, path, query, and fragment: https://learn.example/react/hooks?level=basic#practice.
hints: Read from left to right and use ://, ?, and # as boundaries.
acceptanceCriteria: Explain the evidence or rule behind the answer.
Complete the attempt before opening the solution.

solution.explanation: scheme https; host learn.example; path /react/hooks; query level=basic; fragment practice.

practice.prompt: Draw or write a six-step journey from entering a URL to seeing a page.
hints: Include one request, one response, parsing, and painting.
acceptanceCriteria: Explain the evidence or rule behind the answer.
Complete the attempt before opening the solution.

solution.explanation: One valid flow is DNS lookup → connection → HTTP request → HTTP response → parse HTML and linked resources → layout and paint. Real browsers can overlap work.

practice.prompt: The HTML loads, but styles.css returns 404. Predict the visible result and name the first panel you would inspect.
hints: HTML has browser defaults even without author CSS.
acceptanceCriteria: Explain the evidence or rule behind the answer.
Complete the attempt before opening the solution.

solution.explanation: The content can still appear with default browser styles. Inspect Network, open the failed CSS request, and correct its URL or server path.

practice.prompt: A page waits for a large script before showing useful content. Give two investigation steps without guessing a fix.
hints: Look for timing and main-thread errors.
acceptanceCriteria: Explain the evidence or rule behind the answer.
Complete the attempt before opening the solution.

solution.explanation: Use Network timing to identify the slow or blocking resource, then Performance or Console to see whether downloading, parsing, or executing the script delays rendering.

practice.prompt: A deployed React app returns 200 for index.html, but its JavaScript bundle is 404. Explain why the page may stay blank and what evidence confirms it.
hints: The HTML shell and application code are separate resources.
acceptanceCriteria: Explain the evidence or rule behind the answer.
Complete the attempt before opening the solution.

solution.explanation: The root HTML can load without the code that mounts React. Network shows the bundle 404, Console usually reports a failed module load, and the root element remains empty.

interviewQuestions.question: What happens after a user enters a URL?
interviewQuestions.answer: Explain DNS and connection at a high level, the HTTP request and response, linked-resource requests, DOM and CSS processing, JavaScript, layout, and paint.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Where would you investigate a slow first render?

interviewQuestions.question: Is the DOM always identical to the downloaded HTML?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Parsing can correct invalid markup, and JavaScript can add, remove, or change nodes after download.
interviewQuestions.followUp: How would you compare the response source with the live DOM?

interviewQuestions.question: What is the practical difference between 404 and 500?
interviewQuestions.answer: 404 means the requested resource was not found or exposed at that URL. 500 means the server failed while handling the request.
interviewQuestions.followUp: What other response details would you inspect?

mastery.policy: Reading the lesson or revealing help is not mastery. Save an attempt first, then prove the idea again without the solution and use it in a fresh situation.

checks.evidence: Explain how browser pages work without copying the lesson.
checks.pass: The explanation uses correct terms and gives one practical reason.

checks.evidence: Complete at least four practice tasks before revealing their solutions.
checks.pass: The saved work meets each acceptance criterion and explains the reasoning.

checks.evidence: Use the lesson in a new small page or debugging case.
checks.pass: The new example works and the learner can explain one decision and one tradeoff.

reviewSchedule.note: Complete these without reopening the lesson. Compare only after saving an answer.

problems.prompt: Write the three most useful rules from How browser pages work.
problems.solution: A good answer states three accurate rules, explains why each matters, and uses at least one concrete example.

problems.prompt: Describe one common how browser pages work mistake and repair it.
problems.solution: Choose one mistake from the lesson, identify its cause, and apply the smallest fix that preserves correct web behavior.

problems.prompt: Teach how browser pages work to a beginner in five sentences.
problems.solution: The explanation should define the idea, show how it works, give a real use, warn about a mistake, and name a way to test it.

problems.prompt: Create a different example from the lesson and explain how you verified it.
problems.solution: The example must use the same core concept in a new context and name observable evidence from the browser or code.

commonMistakes.symptom: Calling the internet and the web the same thing
commonMistakes.cause: The web uses internet networking, but they are not identical.
commonMistakes.fix: Say which layer you mean: connection, DNS, HTTP, browser, or server.

commonMistakes.symptom: Assuming a 200 response means the page works
commonMistakes.cause: The response can succeed while JavaScript later throws an error.
commonMistakes.fix: Check Network first, then Console and rendered DOM.

commonMistakes.symptom: Blaming React for every blank screen
commonMistakes.cause: The entry script or another resource may not have loaded.
commonMistakes.fix: Check the document, script requests, Console errors, and root element in order.
